newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin promises wages and pensions in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin promises wages and pensions in 1997.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin thanked Russians for helping him overcome a communist election challenge and severe heart problems over the past year and promised to make their lives easier by paying wages and pensions on time in 1997.

In a message recorded for broadcast first in the far east and then in each of Russia's 10 other time zones, Yeltsin, back in the Kremlin after his quintuple heart bypass surgery in November, said that 1996 had been difficult but important.

"I am grateful to you for having faith in me and for supporting me at the presidential elections; I am grateful to you for your personal participation in helping me to conquer my illness. I consider it my duty, and my business, to respond to your support and to your trust," Yeltsin said.

More than 53 percent of voters backed Yeltsin in the July poll, against 41 percent for his communist rival, after the Kremlin leader pledged big hand-outs to those who have lost out from Russia's market reforms.
But few of the pledges materialised and a tax collection crisis has left millions without cash for months on end.

"The most important thing for me in the New Year is to ensure that life is better and more tranquil for the Russian people, that there should be no more delay in the payment of pensions and wages and that there should at last be order in our country," Yeltsin said.
Seated at a desk alongside the Russian flag, a festive fir tree and a white clock showing a few minutes to twelve, Yeltsin said he hoped next year would be marked by cooperation.
"We all want to live in peace and harmony. In order to achieve this, we should leave behind all our quarrels and squabbles. Let them vanish with the outgoing year."
